w: Dr. Geurs taught this session in class, the week after Dr. Litz's resective surgery lecture (he would rather have gone first: "your first thought should be regeneration"). It is his favorite lecture, and he gave it two goals: recognize periodontal defects that are amenable to regeneration, regrowing the tissues that were lost, and understand what you can expect from therapy. You won't be taught to do the surgery as an entry-level general dentist (it takes specific expertise, the kind a periodontics residency gives); what he wants from you is to spot these defects, know what regeneration can do for the tooth's prognosis, and refer. These notes follow the class, with his slide deck and the class exam-review guide. What regeneration means Periodontal regeneration is the formation of new bone, new cementum and new periodontal ligament, together a new functional attachment apparatus, over a pathologically exposed root surface (the 1996 World Workshop's definition, on the slides). In class: "three different tissues that have to all regenerate in harmony with each other. It can't just be bone alone." If only bone came back, something else would sit between the bone and the root: epithelium, or ligament that isn't attached. The slide sets regeneration against repair, healing that does not restore the original architecture and function. After a flap or root planing, a root usually heals by repair: a long junctional epithelium lies against the root instead of new cementum with inserting ligament fibers, and a pocket lined by epithelium is a pocket again. First, a clean root His opening case was a molar with a deep vertical (infrabony) defect, the two words for the same thing: they describe the shape of bone loss that wraps down beside the root, and with it comes a deep pocket. The first problem in that defect is bacteria. The root wasn't smooth: there was calculus on it, and wherever there is calculus there are bacteria. Calculus is porous and hard to clean, and it lets the pathogenic red and orange complex bacteria sit straight on the root, without the early colonizers a biofilm normally needs first. So the contamination has to go, and the way to clean a root is scaling and root planing ("If you want to answer a question right in perio, the answer is scaling and root planing"). Usually it is done closed first; at the regenerative procedure the flap gives direct access to see the roots and finish cleaning them. "The most important thing to understand is that it has to be clean." How do you know root planing is done? You watch what the tissue does. That is a difference from restorative work, which you can judge the moment you finish (caries out, a restoration that fits, the occlusion right). Periodontal therapy changes the bacteria, and the patient's tissue response does the rest: once the inflammation is no longer needed, it goes away. The soft tissue in the defect isn't PDL (that's gone) and isn't bone. It is granulomatous tissue, the diseased tissue (granulation tissue is the healing tissue, a different thing). It has to be removed: left in place it won't turn into bone or support and it gets in the way of bone healing into the site. Removing it exposes the bony walls of the defect, and those walls can then contribute to healing a site that is new and has to fill with tissue. The race for the space If you simply raise a flap, clean the defect and suture the flap back, "whatever tissue is the fastest in migrating into that defect will win the race to the space." That is the flap's epithelium: it migrates straight down the root toward the bone faster than anything else, and the flap's connective tissue is faster than bone too. Bone heals slowly but very predictably, as long as it isn't moving: a broken leg in a cast heals in about six weeks, where a cut in the skin is gone in a week, and an implant held still by its threads integrates. If epithelium reaches the base of the defect, the result is a pocket again, where bacteria thrive out of reach of the patient's and your cleaning. So regeneration means excluding epithelium and helping the slow tissues win. There are many ways to influence that wound: influence the cells (keep epithelium out, so bone and ligament come back), drug therapy, even gene therapy (turning on genes that drive bone healing, studied in patients who form large exostoses), though drug and gene approaches haven't worked well in periodontal regeneration yet. Simplified, it takes the deck's four factors in periodontal repair and regeneration: cells, a scaffold for them to migrate over (cells may not cross an empty space; a bone graft is one scaffold, artificial or a processed donor product), growth factors, and a blood supply to keep it alive. Platelet-derived growth factor is one growth factor: platelets burst in a wound and release it, telling everything around to heal, so cells survive longer, are more active and migrate faster. Placed in a defect it influences the bone, but also any granulomatous tissue left behind and the soft tissue of the flap. Bone carries growth factors of its own: debriding it releases some locally, though not enough to reach across the whole distance between a bony wall and the root, which a graft can help amplify. The deck's map of strategies (Wang, 2022) splits the field into tissue engineering, which brings cells in (cells grown outside the body, cell aggregates, cells seeded onto scaffolds, even 3D printed), and endogenous regeneration, which adds no cells and draws the patient's own to the site (cell homing) with biological factors, matrix, exosomes or drugs. Grafts, membranes and biologics work with the patient's own cells; an autograft may bring a few of them along. Which defects regenerate: the walls, the angle and the depth Infrabony defects are classified by the number of bony walls, their width and their depth (Reynolds, AAP Regeneration Workshop, 2015). Everything surrounded by three walls is a 3-wall defect, and almost every defect is a combination. In the opening case, once debrided: about 3 mm of 3-wall defect at the base (bone on the facial and lingual there), then about 4 to 6 mm of 2-wall defect with no facial wall, and a 1-wall component coronal to the lingual wall. Each part contributes to how the defect can heal, and a 1-wall defect between two teeth is a hemiseptum. The walls matter because the more walls there are, the more contained the defect: what you put in it stays there, and there is more bony surface to influence the wound. "Potentially the most amenable to regeneration are the three wall defects, the most contained ones." The angle of the walls matters too: a steeper, narrower defect fills more completely, but it is harder to instrument, so there is an optimum between the two. And so does the depth: a shallow defect may regenerate, but other therapies may be more predictable for it. His summary: "more walls, better. An angle that is more steep is better. And the depth of the defect is also important." Flat or horizontal bone loss isn't amenable to regeneration: "There's just no defect to fill." The slide behind that summary gives the numbers: defects with a depth greater than 3 mm and a radiographic defect angle of 25 degrees or less were reported to be most amenable to conventional GTR-based regeneration; non-supportive anatomy, a predominantly 1-wall defect, is a risk factor for failure; and a 1-wall rather than a 2-wall defect and a thin, scalloped gingival biotype were the risk factors for more recession at the midfacial after minimally invasive regenerative surgery. He said the slide's list of studies is there as his sources, "not there for you to read all these studies": know what they support. A 2021 systematic review on the next slide (Nibali) agrees: deeper defects with narrower angles and more walls gained more CAL and radiographic bone 12 months after regenerative surgery. Furcations are a different story. A furcation defect has a bony base, and the rest of it is root surface. A clean root lets tissue migrate over it, but it never contributes cells: it is "kind of a dead surface in healing," which makes furcations harder to treat. Finding the defect before surgery You don't raise a flap to decide whether a defect can be regenerated: you decide from clinical measurements and radiographs. The chart gives the probing depths and, if the gingival margin is recorded, the attachment levels, so you know where the deep pockets are. Radiographs show defects differently than you might think. For bone loss to be obvious to the eye on a film, more than 50% of the mineral content has to be lost, and for most periodontal defects that means the buccal or lingual wall is gone: "by the time we see it on the radiograph, it likely is not a three-wall defect." The defects that are really good for regeneration are the ones that probe deep (an 8 mm pocket, say) where the radiograph shows only a faint shadow. A radiograph is a flat picture of a three-dimensional defect, as the deck's dry-skull films of 3-, 2- and 1-wall defects on the same molar show (Zengin, 2015), so the walls are confirmed at surgery, once the flap is raised and the defect is debrided. Risk assessment and the decision tree The periodontal regeneration risk assessment for intrabony defects (Levine, 2023), which he called a good summary of where your risk is, rates four groups of factors as low, medium or high risk. Patient factors: medical status (healthy, uneventful healing is low; compromised healing is high); smoking (a nonsmoker is low, a light smoker of 10 cigarettes a day or fewer is medium, more than 10 a day is high); plaque control by full-mouth plaque score (15% or less is low, 16 to 24% medium, 25% or more high); compliance with supportive periodontal care (compliant, erratic or poor); and realistic or unrealistic expectations. Tooth factors: the site's periodontal risk score; whether occlusal trauma and mobility are controllable; the endodontic condition (a vital tooth whose defect doesn't reach the apex, or adequate root canal treatment, is low; existing root canal therapy needs careful evaluation and is medium; a defect reaching the apex of a vital tooth, inadequate root canal treatment or a nonvital tooth is high); the root surface (flat is low, concave medium, two fused roots high); intact soft tissue or soft-tissue defects; and the gingival phenotype (thick is low; thin with a band of keratinized tissue 2 mm or wider is medium; thin with a narrow band or none is high). Defect factors: a 3-wall, narrow, deep defect is low, a 2-wall defect medium, and a 1-wall, wide, shallow defect high; no furcation involvement is low, Class I or II medium, Class III high; the defect must be cleansable through surgical access (anterior is low, posterior medium); and a contained defect, with 1 or 2 sides of the root involved, is low, while a non-contained defect, with 3 or more sides involved, is high. Operator factors: experience, environmental stress, and whether a checklist is used. The decision tree from the AAP Regeneration Workshop (Reynolds, 2015) is in the handout, and he told the class to study it. What it says: understand your defect, how deep the pocket is, what the bony morphology is and how many walls it has, and then choose the therapy. It starts with the patient: address first uncontrolled systemic conditions, tobacco use and other behavioral issues, and inadequate oral hygiene (the same factors that ruled furcation regeneration out in Session 5). After initial therapy and any occlusal trauma or mobility management, assess the site: probing depth and CAL, bleeding on probing, mobility and fremitus, the osseous architecture clinically and on radiographs, and any restorative, endodontic or orthodontic work. An intrabony defect under 3 mm isn't a regeneration case: with probing depths of 5 mm or less and no bleeding, consider non-surgical management; with probing depths over 5 mm, consider osseous surgery. For a defect of 3 mm or more, predictability runs 3-wall, then circumferential or 2-wall, then 1-wall, and narrow beats wide. If the prognosis with treatment is unfavorable, or poor to hopeless, the answer is extraction and tooth replacement. Otherwise regeneration follows the defect: a 3-wall or circumferential defect under 2 mm wide takes a bone graft, a GTR membrane or a biologic; one 3 mm or wider, or a 2-wall defect, takes a reinforced GTR membrane, a bone graft plus a GTR membrane, or a bone graft plus a biologic; a 1-wall defect takes combination therapy or a cellular bone allograft. Esthetic risk is weighed alongside. With low risk (a low smile line, a thick biotype, a full papilla, under 5 mm from the contact to the interproximal bone crest), proceed. With high risk (a high smile line, a thin biotype, papilla loss or more than 6 mm from the contact to the crest), proceed only if the patient accepts the esthetic risk, avoid a GTR membrane, and consider soft-tissue augmentation. The toolbox, and the baseline it has to beat The deck lists the options: bone grafts, guided tissue regeneration (GTR), combination therapy, biomodification with growth factors (enamel matrix protein, PDGF) and the surgical technique itself: MIST, the minimally invasive surgical technique, which works through a small flap that keeps the papilla. The most important thing is that the root is clean and that you understand what you put in the defect and how it should contribute to healing. Regenerative therapy rebuilds the lost support; resective therapy, from Session 5, takes what is there and makes it maintainable by eliminating the pocket. Surgical technique, to him, is the most important parameter. Most of dentistry's evidence is paid for by industry and is about a product someone sells, so there is plenty on bone grafts and barrier membranes and little on surgical technique: how you get the tissue out of the way, get enough access to clean the defect and see what it looks like, put something in it, and close it while disrupting the blood supply as little as possible. "Open the door, put stuff in, close the door." The less you open, the more of the blood supply stays. The baseline is open flap debridement. Open the defect, clean it and close it, and it heals one way or another: a little bone fill at the base (most likely in the 3-wall part at the bottom) and a little attachment gain, so "we're almost guaranteed by just cleaning it out to get a millimeter." Whatever is added has to outperform that. Across four studies on the slide (Froum 1981, Renvert 1985, Yukna 1985 and Laurell's 1998 meta-analysis), defects 3.4 to 4.3 mm deep started at probing depths of about 6.3 to 7.4 mm and ended at about 3.5 to 4.1 mm, with 1.3 to 1.5 mm of CAL gain and 0.7 to 1.2 mm of bone gain; Laurell's 305 defects went from 7.0 to 4.0 mm with 1.5 mm of CAL gain and 1.1 mm of bone gain. The probing depth fell 3 mm but the attachment level only 1.5 mm, because the rest of the pocket reduction is recession. It is historical data: other therapies now do much better. Bone grafts: the canine case A mandibular canine next to the lateral incisor had a vertical defect. It had a root canal with two canals, which is uncommon in a mandibular canine, and two canals mean two roots formed and fused together, usually into an H-shaped root with a concavity. At surgery, through a small "peekaboo" flap, the defect was what the radiograph suggested, a 3-wall component and a 2-wall component, and in the concavity was a streak of calculus: a hard place for the patient to clean, and the reason the defect was there. The root canal wasn't why the tooth could be regenerated. You don't need a root canal to do regeneration: "generally for a tooth to do regeneration, all you need is clean roots." A root canal is done when the tooth's vitality is compromised, as it may be when a defect reaches toward the apex. The defect was filled with DFDBA, demineralized freeze-dried bone allograft: donor bone, ground into particles and demineralized to expose the bone morphogenetic protein embedded in it. So it is a scaffold for bone to grow over and also a growth factor that calls bone in, and the body recognizes it and remodels it as bone. The flap was pulled back over it and sutured, because contamination is still a risk and the flap protects the graft and the clot, and the tooth wasn't moving: like a broken bone, a defect heals when it is still. Sometimes he skips initial therapy before a case like this, because root planing first tightens the tissue and leaves less soft tissue volume to cover the graft. The result (1993) was a shallow, maintainable pocket, and on the radiograph the defect filled in: a vertical defect became a horizontal one. That is the expectation, to fill the defect, not to grow bone back to within 1.5 mm of the CEJ where it belongs. It changed the tooth's prognosis, and a canine is worth it: the canine is "the cornerstone of the dentition," giving canine guidance so the laterals and posterior teeth aren't stressed ("canines are gold"). Because of the concavity, this patient should use an interdental brush, whose bristles spread into it, rather than floss, which bridges over the concavity and misses its depth. Guided tissue regeneration and combination therapy GTR sets up the race for the space. The potential to heal is in the defect: bone, and a little ligament space at the base, but those are the slow tissues; the fast ones are in the flap. So a barrier membrane goes between the defect and the flap, keeping out the flap's epithelium and connective tissue and letting the tissues we want repopulate the wound and decide what it becomes. The classic studies of the early 1980s wrapped laboratory filters around teeth and showed that bone could grow back; when he went to dental school, he was taught it couldn't. Early membranes had to be taken back out; today's collagen barriers are bioabsorbed: they stay a while, influence the healing and go away. His patient Jeffrey had a deep defect (a 10 mm pocket) and an exostosis on the facial of the same quadrant. Dr. Geurs took off the exostosis, harvested the patient's own bone from it, packed it into the defect and covered it with a membrane: combination therapy, a scaffold (and possibly some cells) in the defect with a membrane over it. A bone graft under a membrane also holds the space, so the membrane can't collapse into the defect. The papilla didn't fully come back: raising tissue off a tooth and putting it back heals with a little recession, especially interproximally, a compromise of this therapy. The defect filled and leveled out, and it was still there on radiographs at 1, 20 and 25 years. On the later films the crest looks dense, sometimes called a crestal lamina dura, which goes with less activity and stability; a fuzzy crest, as before treatment, means activity and resorption. (Seeing Jeffrey every three months for years, his team was also the first to notice his cognitive decline: dentists see patients more often than physicians do.) The patient's own bone is used particulated, scraped off as bone dust or ground in a bone mill, and not processed, because it is the patient's own tissue. Fresh bone transplanted from another person, as was done in the 1970s, transmitted disease; with today's processed donor grafts, disease transmission isn't documented. Some clinicians add antibiotics to harvested bone, but a good blood clot does that job itself. Is autogenous bone better? "My conventional thinking was always yes, but the evidence doesn't really support that": a processed donor graft exposes its bone morphogenetic protein better and goes in clean, while harvested bone can carry contamination. It's a toss-up; he likes the patient's own bone because it's already there and the patient doesn't pay for a bottle. Biologics Enamel matrix derivative (EMD) goes back to embryology and Hertwig's epithelial root sheath. Its proteins, mostly amelogenins, the proteins of enamel formation and periodontal attachment formation during tooth development, are harvested from the developing teeth of miniature swine, a species genetically close to us (in humans they could only come from a developing wisdom tooth), then processed. Applied to a defect they set off a healing cascade like development, and he has seen "amazing healing" from EMD alone, without a bone graft. Alone or with a graft, EMD gives outcomes similar to GTR. Because it is porcine-derived, the patient has to be told and has to consent (it has been discussed with leaders of religions that avoid pork, but it is each patient's decision). The same goes for any donor product: say what you are using and why, call it a processed donor product, note that disease transmission isn't documented with these grafts, and let the patient say yes or no. A colleague who placed donor dermis in a priest without telling him had to take it out again. One of his EMD cases, from 2022, had almost no bone left and was very mobile. "Mobility is not a good thing during healing": a tooth that moves won't heal, like a leg out of its cast. So he splinted it with composite on the lingual, then placed EMD in the defect. The patient never came back for maintenance until a wisdom tooth abscess in 2025, and the bone was still there; the tooth, which had been slightly super-erupted, needed only a little occlusal adjustment. Splinting and regeneration together saved a tooth that might not have survived a treatment-planning session. Dr. Litz, as a resident, treated the opening case with Dr. Geurs: EMD on the root and mixed into a DFDBA graft that filled the defect, with the flap closed over it. At two and a half months the radiograph showed little, because a demineralized allograft has no calcium and doesn't show until the body heals around it; later films showed the fill. There was some recession, mostly over the parts that had been 1-wall. With the fill, the result was a shallow pocket: a maintainable tooth, though a harder area to clean, where food traps. From the exam-review guide: rhPDGF-BB, recombinant human platelet-derived growth factor BB, is chemotactic and mitogenic for bone and PDL cells and angiogenic, so it drives revascularization; it is paired with a beta-TCP scaffold, an osteoconductive matrix that keeps soft tissue from collapsing into the defect and stabilizes the clot. Grafts are named by where they come from: an autograft from the patient, an allograft from another human (DFDBA), a xenograft from another species, such as bovine bone, and an alloplast, a synthetic material such as beta-tricalcium phosphate. Non-contained defects. The deck gives a slide to treating non-contained infrabony defects (Journal of Periodontology, 2017), following one case from the radiograph through the flap, debridement, the graft packed into the defect and the sutures to the follow-up film. Without walls, nothing holds up the flap or the clot, so a biologic alone has little space to work in; these defects usually get a graft as well, to support the soft tissue, which is why the decision tree sends a 1-wall defect to combination therapy. A tooth or an implant? Why not take the tooth out and place an implant? Implants are predictable, but "a natural tooth is almost always better than an implant, unless you can't keep the tooth." A regenerated tooth may last another 20 or 30 years, postponing an implant until there may be better therapy, and it keeps later options open (a mesio-occlusal restoration can still become a crown, a root canal can still be done). When an implant fails, the patient says your implant isn't working, and treating one failure can absorb the revenue of the next seven implant cases. Patients don't want implants, they want teeth, and many teeth that could be regenerated don't survive treatment planning in practice. A periodontist only gets to treat these defects when a general dentist recognizes them and refers. What can you achieve, and how do you know? The deck's results slide shows four combinations healing on radiographs over 3 to 16 months: Emdogain with DFDBA, GTR with autogenous bone, rhPDGF with DFDBA, and DFDBA alone. Every one started as a vertical defect, and DFDBA, the patient's own bone or the two combined can all result in regeneration, if the surgical technique is right. Regeneration is evaluated three ways: histology, clinical measurements and radiographs. "The real evaluation of regeneration should be histological," but very few patients allow it, so clinical measurements and radiographs serve as surrogates. Only histology, a section of the tooth with its surrounding tissue, can show new cementum with inserting PDL fibers and new bone, and so prove true regeneration; a probe can't tell new attachment from a long junctional epithelium, and a radiograph shows bone fill, not attachment. Digital subtraction radiography takes two standardized radiographs from different times, inverts one and overlays it on the other, so everything that stayed the same cancels out and only what changed shows. It is the work that brought him to Birmingham. Dr. Geurs and colleagues used it to evaluate a bioresorbable membrane (Chaves, Geurs, Reddy and Jeffcoat, 1996): the subtraction image lit up the bone gained between the presurgical film and the one at 6 months. In that study, a patient with a hopeless tooth agreed to have its defect regenerated, then the tooth removed for an implant: a notch cut in the root at the calculus, where there had been no bone, showed new PDL, new bone and a little new cementum. Histological evidence of regeneration in a human. At high magnification the new ligament isn't quite the ligament around a healthy tooth, but it is functional and resists breakdown over time. So, his two objectives. When can you regenerate? Vertical defects: deep, contained, with walls. What can you expect? Fill of the defect and a shallower, maintainable pocket, which changes the tooth's prognosis. Look for these defects in practice and keep teeth as long as you can.
